headline: Powerful Thanksgiving storm threatens East Coast with floods, damaging winds
author: Tim Craig, Matthew Cappucci

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — The East Coast could experience its worst Thanksgiving storm in decades on Thursday as forecasters and local officials warn that strong winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding could severely impede travel and lead to prolonged power outages.

The large storm is expected to progress through the Mid-Atlantic region during the day, resulting in high wind and flood warnings from Virginia Beach to New York City, as well as possibly damaging conditions in Washington, Baltimore and Philadelphia.

The storm forced the postponement of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday, the first time in its 100-year history that the event was moved due to weather. Officials said they made the decision because of concerns that participants and spectators would encounter dangerous conditions.
“Safety is and always will be our top priority,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said during a Wednesday news conference with Macy’s. “And this will be a heavy storm.”
Philadelphia also canceled its Thanksgiving Day parade.
On Wednesday evening, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) issued a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.

In New Jersey, all 21 counties are also under a state of emergency after Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) warned that residents faced a “serious storm that requires us all to exercise caution.” Sherrill urged residents to complete their holiday travel on Wednesday night and stay off the roads on Thursday during the worst of the storm.
In Delaware, Gov. Matt Meyer (D) said residents should keep cellphones charged and have flashlights, extra food and medications handy.
“Be ready for power outages and difficult travel,” Meyer said in a statement Wednesday evening. “Adjust your plans if you need to and follow instructions from emergency officials.”

The storm system is poised to clobber portions of the Mid-Atlantic and the Northeast with the potential for winds near hurricane force in beach communities. Farther inland, winds could reach 60 mph, including along the Interstate 95 corridor.
Officials warned that outages could stretch into the weekend if the winds bring down trees and power lines.

In some coastal communities, the National Weather Service forecast that major flooding was possible. Coastal flood warnings were in effect for the entire New Jersey coastline and most of Delmarva, the Chesapeake, the mouth of the Hudson River and southern Long Island.
A storm surge of 2 to 4 feet is likely. The National Weather Service warned that some neighborhoods could be “cut off at the peak of the flooding.”

Sherrill said flooding in southern New Jersey could “match or exceed” the height of waters that inundated beach towns during a September nor’easter. That storm severely eroded beaches and flooded some homes and businesses.
“The coastal flooding [Thursday] could be especially intense because high winds will coincide with high tide” said Sherrill, adding the worst flood risks are expected Thursday morning.
The instigating storm system organized over Florida on Wednesday evening and it was energized, and steered westward, by an approaching upper-air disturbance.

The storm swung north toward the Carolinas overnight, bringing gusty onshore winds, very heavy downpours and thunderstorms. As the system moves into the Mid-Atlantic on Thursday, strong winds are likely.
The low-pressure center will trek north up the Appalachians, much farther inland than conventional East Coast storms.

The strengthening low-pressure system will produce winds of more than 80 mph about 2,500 feet above the ground. Severe gusts are likely at those altitudes, and any downpours or possible thunderstorms would effectively push those strong winds toward the ground.
The heaviest rains and greatest wind potential will affect D.C., Baltimore, Philadelphia, Delaware and New Jersey late Thursday morning into the afternoon.
Mamdani said the rain could lead to flash flooding, and he urged residents who live in low-lying neighborhoods or basement apartments to closely monitor conditions.

Widespread 50- to 60-mph gusts are possible, and high-resolution computer models suggest a few 70 to 75 mph gusts at the immediate coastline. New York officials have barred high-profile vehicles and trucks without cargo from seven major bridges due to concerns they could be blown over.
Winds will be less dramatic in New England when the heavy rains arrive Thursday evening, though Cape Cod, Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard could see a few gusts topping 50 mph.

The same storm system will also dump snow in eastern Missouri and western Illinois. A winter storm warning is in effect for St. Louis, where 3 to 6 inches of snow is likely. A few locations west of the city could see as much as 6 to 10 inches of snow.

The storm center will be more than 600 miles to the southeast when the snow begins early Thursday. But a weak, diffuse strip of secondary low pressure — known as an “inverted trough” — will protrude to the northwest and generate the snow.
The storm system will gradually weaken Friday as it swirls remnant rain and mountain snow showers over the Ohio Valley and northern Appalachians.
Improving weather and sunshine are likely in the Northeast on Saturday.
